The NAME stays public: the phase's surface promise is additive, the pipeline law family states its minimal re-invocation law over it, and the Capability model's oracle differential names it; it is a one-line forward, not a second closure. Whether the Capability model's own `dirtySet` section is re-stated as an instance of `Propagation.fst`'s closure is a proof-design question and is not decided here.

**D173.3 — the capture-key grammars are three, as data, behind one builder (Phase 225's grammars recorded).** `Hash.keyedBy prefix fields` is `prefix + "#" + fnv1a (canonicalFields fields)`, and every capture key is it over its own field list:

| Key | Prefix | Fields |
|---|---|---|
| `Capability.invocationKey` | the capability id | per binding, addr-sorted: addr, the value in its hole's canonical spelling (2 fields) |
| `Query.invocationKey` | the query id | `QueryShape.keyFields` (`""`,`w`,filter / `""`,`o`,order, each when non-empty), then per binding, name-sorted: name, cell tag (`i f b s d t m n`), payload (3 fields) |
| `Query.invocationKeyPage` | the query id | `""`,`p`,token, then `invocationKey`'s fields; `None` is `invocationKey` |
| `CapabilityPipeline.nodeInvocationKey` | `source#<id>` / `<capId>#<id>` | `source`,id,dref / `invoke`,capId,id, then per binding addr,`L`/`N`,value, the triples ordered by their encoded pre-image |

The grammars stay three (operator ruling 2026-10-17, item 3A): unifying them moves every journal. Recording them as data behind one builder moves none: the bytes were recorded from the build before the change and are pinned literally in `QueryTests` and `FunctionTests`, beside `conformance/laws/capability-laws.json`'s capability keys; the `invocation_key_*` theorems are about the field encodings, which did not change. `invocationKeyPage`'s body is no longer a copy of `invocationKey`'s: both read one private field list. The key roster's family counts a call of `keyedBy` as a call of the encoding, and holds `keyedBy`'s own body to `canonicalFields` both by reading it and by running it, so the widening admits no key that leaves the encoding.

**D173.4 — one evaluator body, over a `Scope`.** `Propagation.Scope<'v>` is `Full | From of prior * changed | For of targets` — WHAT an evaluation computes — and `evalScopedWith evalNode scope plan` / `evalScoped` evaluate it over a prepared `Plan`. The redesign pass sketched a fourth case, `FromPlan`, beside a `deps` argument; that would carry the graph twice (the plan holds its map), so the graph is the `Plan` argument and the plan axis leaves the scope. The eight named entry points forward to the one private body with their behaviour to the byte, each scope held equal to the entry point it names, result and evaluation order, in `PropagationTests`; the named forms that never push (`eval`, `evalFor` and their `With` forms) still invert no map. They stay public — the UI tier calls them — and `propagationLaws` is unchanged. The scoped pair are new names, not a retyping of `eval` / `evalWith`, because this phase's surface is additive.

**D173.5 — `AiSurface`: one guarded form per verb, and a typed `runTool` refusal.** `Proposals.submit` / `approve` and `submitGuarded` / `approveGuarded` were four bodies; they are two private bodies over a decision function and an optional dry run, and the four public verbs keep their signatures: the unguarded verbs are the bodies with the surface's `Decide` and no dry run, the guarded ones with `decideGuarded` and `DryRun`. The approver's refusal is the sequence's joined decision (`PolicyDecision.all`, first denial wins), which is the first denial the previous `tryPick` found. `aiSurfaceLawsAt` and `policyLawsAt` hold both paths. `AiSurface.tryRunTool` refuses as `ReadToolFailure.UnknownReadTool(name, available)`, beside the unchanged string form, whose sentence is `ReadToolFailure.describe`. The seams' vocabulary was considered for it and not used: read tools are a frozen witness list, not a `Seam`, and a read is not policy-admitted, so the refusal takes the vocabulary's `NoSuch` SHAPE (the id and every held id) without a seam to carry it.

## 2026-10-19 — D172: the seam dispatch prologue is written once, over a vocabulary, and published as `Seam`; the decoder helpers the seam codecs shared are Wire's; amends D117.2 and D118.7

**Status:** Live

**Recorded by Phase 509.** `Fuaran.Core.Function` (`KeyedRegistry.fs`, `Capability.fs`, `FunctionRegistry.fs`, `CapabilityPipeline.fs`, `SeamCodec.fs`), `Fuaran.Core.Query` (`QueryRegistry.fs`, `FunctionInternals.fs`, `Query.fs`, `QueryCodec.fs`), `Fuaran.Core.Wire` (`Decoder.fs`); rides the `0.39.0` draft (docs/releases/0.39.0.md, Additive). The `api/` baselines of `Function` and `Wire` gain members and lose none; `Query`'s does not move. No refusal sentence, `$type` tag or journal byte moves.

**Context.** The three id-keyed registries shared the lattice (D117.2) and nothing else. The prologue every dispatch verb runs — resolve the id, else `NoSuch…(id, known)`; validate; admit through the policy; settle the body — was written out at eleven verbs, the `known` list built inline fourteen times, `decide` three times, and the two journalled shapes (Phase 318) once per seam, body for body. The duplication audit of 2026-10-16 found a host's capability invoker (fuaran#2310) that had hand-rolled the same prologue outside this repository and skipped the policy gate: the shape it needed was internal, so it wrote its own.

**D172.1 — D117.2 is widened from the lattice to dispatch (amends D117.2).** `KeyedRegistry` (still internal) gains `resolve`, `admit`, `decide`, `dispatch`, `dispatchCaptured` and `dispatchReplayed`, over a `SeamVocabulary` — the seam's refusal constructors, its admission gate and its argument check. The capability and query registries' verbs forward to it through `Seam` (D172.2); `FunctionRegistry`'s `decide` and `dispatch` call it directly, with the capability seam's vocabulary and `_.Capability` as the declaration its gates read. `FunctionRegistry` is not a `Seam`: its entries carry a result kind beside the capability, and its public `withGate` takes a gate over `Capability`, so a `Seam` over `FunctionEntry` would need every gate re-wrapped, and a re-wrapped gate is a new closure, which `RegistryPolicy`'s by-reference equality would read as a different policy. The `known` lists are `KeyedRegistry.ids`, once. D117.2's reasons for leaving the validator registry off the lattice stand; whether it joins is Phase 521's ruling.

**D172.2 — the shape is published (amends D118.7).** `Seam<'Decl,'Args,'E>` is public and opaque: the declarations by id, the `RegistryPolicy` every invocation passes, and the vocabulary it answers in. Its module carries the lattice (`register`, `tryFind`, `enumerate`, `ids`, `unregister`, `replace`, `restrict`, `union`), the gate (`withGate`, `onDenied`, `decide`) and the three dispatch shapes; there is no public verb that runs a declaration without admitting it. D118.7 kept the helper internal because the gate lived in `RegistryPolicy` and did not need it published; the audit finding is why that no longer holds — a public gate with a private prologue let a host build the prologue without the gate. `CapabilityRegistry` and `QueryRegistry` are each a `Seam` behind their unchanged public verbs, so the published shape is the one Core's own seams run, not a parallel copy. `resolve` and `admit` stay internal: published separately, they would let an adopter resolve and run without admitting, which is the defect the publication closes.

**D172.3 — two records, the vocabulary and the capture.** `SeamVocabulary` holds what every seam needs (`Id`, `NoSuch`, `Duplicate`, `Admission`, `Validate`, `Refused`, `Approval`, `Describe`). `SeamCapture` holds what only a journalling dispatch needs: the determinism `Label`, the invocation `Key`, and the pair that writes a refusal the body answered into the journal and reads it back (`Record`, `Read`). It is an argument of the two journalled verbs, not a field of the seam, because the key may read more than the arguments: the query seam's paged verbs key on the page token, and pass a capture built for that page. The body a dispatch runs answers `Result<Deferred<'r>,'E>`, so a body can refuse in the seam's own error (the query resolver's `ResolveFault`s do); the capability seam's body answers `Deferred`, settled through `InvokeError.settle`, whose only refusal is `BodyFailed m`, which it records as `m` and reads back as `BodyFailed m` — the bytes it journalled before.

**D172.4 — a seam is equal by its vocabulary's identity.** `Seam` compares its declarations structurally, its policy by `RegistryPolicy`'s equality, and its vocabulary by reference, as a policy compares its gates. A registry built from one vocabulary value is equal to itself through every lattice round trip (`unregister` after `register`), which `RegistryLifecycleTests` holds; two vocabularies that happen to agree are two seams.

**D172.5 — every `Seam` verb is `NoInlining`.** Each body reads the seam's private representation or this package's internal `KeyedRegistry`, and `QueryRegistry` calls them from another package. D129's check reads the built assemblies and found no site in Release with the attribute removed from `register` and `tryFind` (the optimiser does not copy a body reading a private representation across packages); the attribute is kept because D129's rule is stated on the attribute, not on the optimiser's present choices. `FunctionInternals.Registry`, the six forwarders through which `QueryRegistry` reached the lattice and the policy's admission, is deleted: the query registry crosses no internal of `Function` any more.

**D172.6 — the decoder helpers are Wire's.** The seam codecs each wrote a closed-set string read in their own sentence (`tagged`, twice, with two forwarders), a two-member combinator (`both`, twice) and a string-array read (`strList`). They are `Decoder.oneOfWith`, `Decoder.pair` and `Decoder.strings`. The first is named for the module's own convention — `oneOf` in the caller's sentence, as `tagDispatchWith` is `tagDispatch` in the caller's sentence — not `tagged`, which in this module would read as a tag dispatch; its body is the codecs' body, so every refusal it answers is the one they answered. Two items the plan listed were already true at HEAD: `Decoder.str` has been Wire's since Phase 310, and the codecs' `let str name = Decoder.field name Decoder.str` is a composition of two public combinators that gets no third name; and `SeamCodec.members` has been `Decoder.members` with the sentence since Phase 388. The `"$type"` dispatch the capability and pipeline codecs both spelled is `SeamCodec.dispatch`, internal. The string-array WRITER the two seams each carry (`strs`) stays where it is: it is an encoder, not a decoder.

**D172.7 — what moved in order, and why nothing observable did.** `CapabilityRegistry.dispatchWithArgs` validated and typed the arguments before the policy, and now validates, admits, then types. Typing an argument that validated cannot fail (`Capability.typeArgs` types with the parses validation made), so the order of a refusal an observer could see is unchanged; validation runs twice on that verb.

## 2026-10-19 — D171: a vector family is one shape and an emitted family is one exporter row; the one writer stays internal until its first outside adopter, and the escape oracle is stated from the rule, not read from the escaper

**Status:** Live

**Recorded by Phase 508.** `Fuaran.Core.Conformance` (`VectorKit.fs`: `VectorFamily`, `CorpusFile`; the five vector modules; `StoredIdentity`), `tests/Fuaran.Core.Tests/Exporters.fs`; rides the `0.39.0` draft (docs/releases/0.39.0.md, Internal). No public surface moves; no byte of a file the corpus copies moves.

*Decided: one vector shape.* `VectorFamily<'V>` is a corpus, a per-vector law name, the checks one vector makes and the line a host diffs; `run`, `check`, `lines`, `laws` and `lawsWith` are written once over it. `WireNullTolerance`, `StringEscapeVectors`, `EncodingProfileVectors` and `ParityVectors` instantiate it, each public entry point keeping its signature and every law its name. `ParityVectors`' laws stay pooled over the table, because uniqueness is a property of the table and not of a row. The stored trio is one walk over a `Store` union (linear chain, DAG, capture log); `linearLaws`, `dagLaws` and `captureLaws` are its three spellings.

*Decided: one exporter table.* Every family the test runner emits is one row of `Exporters.table`; every file is written by `CorpusFile.render`, which escapes through `Canon.render`; every self-enumerated manifest is `CorpusManifest`; every committed file is held to its row by one reading, `CorpusFile.firstDifference`. `--emit <family>` dispatches over the table, and the `--emit-<family>` spellings stay as aliases, because `copies.json`, the projection registry and the shared corpus's producer record quote them.

*Decided: the machinery is internal.* `VectorFamily`, the `Store` union and `CorpusFile` are internal to the Conformance assembly. A public generic runner returning `LawResult list` would read to the roster as a law family, and a public writer published ahead of the consumer that adopts it would freeze a contract before anyone has used it. The writer is published in the change-set in which a second producer drops its own hand writer and adopts it, with that consumer in the same change (D51).

*Decided: the control-character table is stated once, from the rule.* The 32 rows both escape tables enumerate are `VectorKit.controlCharacters`, written from the rule's statement. The redesign pass proposed reading them from `Wire.Json`'s own table; that would make the oracle the code it judges, so every change to the escaper would agree with itself. `Wire.Json` exposes nothing new.

*Cost.* `WireNullTolerance`'s per-vector counterexample now reads `<vector name>: <detail>`, the shape every other vector family's has. `conformance/refusals/manifest.json` and `conformance/decode/manifest.json` move onto the apply manifest's shape (the adoption map spaced, in roster order); neither is copied into the corpus.

Each old name stays as an `Obsolete` forward with its own roster row until the 1.0 retirement, so no id disappears. A consumer census adds a row for each new stem at its next raise.

## 2026-10-18 — D168: a clone holding no release tag reads as "no released tag" and the tag-reading families skip it by name; a clone holding release tags that HEAD's history does not contain is red

**Status:** Live

**Recorded by Phase 502.** `tests/Fuaran.Core.Tests/ChildProcess.fs` (`Tags.released`); `CONTRIBUTING.md`; rides the `0.39.0` draft (docs/releases/0.39.0.md, Internal).

*Decided: two states, not one.* Phase 499 made a tagless clone fail the release-record check and the two package-roster tag checks, on the ground that an empty tag set passes them vacuously. That ground conflated two states, which Phase 502 separates:
- `ChildProcess.Tags.released` returns `Error NoReleaseTag` when `git tag --list` holds no `vX.Y.Z` tag at all (a fork, or a clone made without tags). Every tag-reading family treats that as a named, counted skip, with the remedy printed.
- It returns an empty set only when release tags exist and HEAD descends from none of them, which no checkout of this history can be. That is a broken reader or a truncated history, and the three vacuity guards stay red on it.

A first clone therefore meets the gate `CONTRIBUTING.md` describes, and the vacuity protection stays where it is needed.

*Cost.* A CI run that lost its tags skips these legs by name rather than failing them. Both workflows pin `fetch-tags: true`.

This amends D123 only in that its `--merged HEAD` reading, which Phase 499 made every tag-reading family's, now has this third answer.

## 2026-10-18 — D166: the pinned over-approximation is a property of the PURE footprint; precision lives where the base is known, computed at the tree the script applies to and threaded through it, and every pair is proved

**Status:** Live

**Recorded by Phase 500.** `src/Fuaran.Core.Ops/Ops.fs` (`footprintIn`, `footprintInKeyed`), `Arbitration.fs` (`arbitrateIn`), `src/Fuaran.Core.OpStream.Dag/DagOpStream.fs` (`conflictsIn`, `reconcileIn`, `reconcileManyIn`), `src/Fuaran.Core.Conformance/ConcurrencyLaws.fs` (`footprintInLawsAt`), `proofs/TreeOps.fst` section 24, `proofs/FootprintIn.fst`, `proofs.json`; rides the `0.39.0` draft (docs/releases/0.39.0.md, Additive).

**Context.** `Ops.footprint` records an unknown-parent write for every remove, move and in-place rewrite, and `Ops.independent` refuses that against every structural write; Phase 143 proved the clause necessary over the `Footprint` record for any footprint computed from the script alone, and Phase 163 named the precondition of a tightening — a footprint that can say which subtree a removal destroys, "which the pure script cannot compute". The first domain to adopt the footprint at scale measured the cost: 84% of its generated auto-merges refused while the fold reaches one tree in either order, because two in-place edits of different nodes anywhere in the tree interfere. The arbitration and the fold both hold the tree the script applies to.

**Decision.** (1) The pinned over-approximations are properties of the PURE form and stay pinned for it; `Ops.footprint`, `footprintKeyed`, `independent` and every pure entry keep their verdicts. (2) Precision lives where the base is known: `Ops.footprintIn` / `footprintInKeyed` compute the same `Footprint` record at the tree the script applies to — a removal or a move names its source parent as a known structure-write and a read, a removal content-writes the subtree it destroys (Phase 163's set), a move reads its destination's ancestors (the cycle check reads them, and a move pair nesting into each other's subtrees is refused through that read where the pure form refused it through the unknown-parent clause), an `UpdateNode` reads and content-writes its target alone, and an absent target takes the pure arm. (3) The script is THREADED: each op is footprinted at the state the ops before it reach, through the engine the script lands with (`apply`; the keyed engine with an admitting container capability for the keyed form), and from an op that does not apply the rest takes the pure arm. Footprinting every op against the one base is UNSOUND and was rejected on a counterexample found while designing the function: a lane that moves `q` under `c` and then removes `c`'s ancestor `x` destroys `q`'s subtree, which the base says nothing about, so a concurrent edit inside `q` read as independent at the base. (4) The entries that hold the base compose it: `Arbitration.arbitrateIn` (the keyed and contained compositions are one `arbitrateWith` call each, documented, not added — the rule of three), `Dag.conflictsIn` (per delta threaded through the caller's `apply`), `Dag.reconcileIn` / `reconcileManyIn`, which replay the SHARED region before any footprint is read, because that is the state the exclusive deltas apply to; the one observable reordering is that a lane set both forms refuse reports `SharedHistoryRejected` where `reconcileMany` reported `LanesInterfere`. (5) `Conformance.footprintInLawsAt` certifies soundness, refinement of the pure projection and determinism at a domain's own ops, guarded on a pair only the base-aware footprint frees. (6) The model is `TreeOps.fst` section 24 (extracted, held to production by the oracle differential, which also shows the comparison is not production against itself); the theorems are a proof-only module, `FootprintIn.fst`, opening `TreeOps` as `Arbitrate.fst` does, because `TreeOps` is the leg's slowest module and a second diamond proof inside it would pass its budget. `footprint_in_refines` is proved whole. `footprint_in_sound` is proved over every operation — inserts, removals, moves, reorders, rewrites and batches of them, lifted along a script with the footprint's STABILITY under an independent op's application, the one fact the pure lift never needed. The remove pairs stand on every id outside a destroyed subtree surviving the removal at the same node under the same parent; the five move pairs (AMENDED IN PLACE 2026-10-18 by the phase's continuation session: the entry as first recorded proved everything but a `MoveNode` and quantified over `no_move`, the boundary written as a predicate as `TreeOps.covered` once was) stand on each edit distributing over a graft at another parent, on the path to a node being kept by every edit that does not relocate it — what keeps the ancestors a move's footprint reads where they were — and on what a move leaves in place: every id, every other node found at the same node with the move applied inside it, every parent but the target's. `no_move` survives only as the name of the intermediate theorem (`footprint_in_sound_no_move`), as `in_place` does for the fragment before it. The cost of the proof: the join of each move pair as ONE prover query sat at the pinned rlimit's edge (three timeouts, then a seed-sensitive pass), so each pair is three small facts and their join, and the module's budget was re-seeded by the roster's rule.

**Consequences.** A consumer adopts by one call per entry and loses no fold (`footprint_in_refines`); the first adopting domain re-measures its 0.84 share against `footprintIn`. The `UpdateNode` arm reads no ancestor path, against the phase's sketch: a removal of an ancestor is caught because the removal content-writes its whole subtree, and a move of an ancestor commutes with an in-place rewrite — the theorem is what says the read is not needed, and reading it would refuse that commuting pair. `Dag.conflictsIn` takes the domain's `apply` where `conflicts` takes none, and `reconcileIn` takes the witness and the base state where `reconcile` takes neither: the footprint is read at a state only a replay reaches. The five move pairs of `footprint_in_sound` were proved in the same phase, so no successor carries them and nothing of the theorem is left to the oracle.

## 2026-10-18 — D165: a ladder row states its claim and its boundary; every proof-leg run leaves one verdict record

**Status:** Live

**Recorded by Phase 522.** `proofs.json`, `proofs/kit/LADDER.md`, `proofs/kit/check-proof-leg.ps1` (`-SummaryFile`, the `proofRunVerdict` record), `proofs/check.ps1`; rides the `0.39.0` draft (docs/releases/0.39.0.md, Internal).

**Context.** `proofs.json` rows carried one free-form `claim` mixing what is claimed, what it does not cover, and how the row came to be; a `tested` row's `family` was free text (three rows carried a sentence) and its cases were looked for across eight enumerated suites whatever the family said; `kit/LADDER.md` documented checks no test performed (`supporting` held like `theorem`; `artifact`, `host` and `document` existing). The proof leg wrote a summary only on a green strict run, and its three readers (the empty cone's baseline, the strict workflow, the refusal tests) each read the run by a different convention, the workflow by grepping the log.

**Decision.** (1) A row carries `statement` (what is claimed) and `boundary` (what it does not cover, never empty); neither tells history: the row's `phase` is its one citation (no `Phase NNN` text in either). `claim` stays, as exactly `statement + " " + boundary`, because the registry reads `claim` and refuses a row without it; the `claim-is-the-join` clause holds the join. When the registry reads the two fields, `claim` is dropped in the same change that drops the clause. (2) A `tested` row's `family` is CLOSED: `Proofs.Oracle`, `Conformance.<law>` (a law the kit exports), or `Suite:<Module>.<list>` (a test list named by its module and value, never by its prose label); its cases must be cases OF that suite, resolved by reflection over the test assembly. (3) Every check `kit/LADDER.md` documents is performed: `supporting` names are top-level in the model; `artifact`, `host` and a policy `document` exist; this repository's family refuses `repo`, because it holds rows to its own tree only. (4) The kit engine's `-SummaryFile` writes ONE run verdict (`kind: proofRunVerdict`) on EVERY exit: the verdict class named (`green`, `refuted`, `aborted`, `apparatus`, `failed`), the exit, the red line, and what the run was; exit codes and printed lines are unchanged. `check.ps1` writes every run's record to `proofs/obj/last-run.json` with its `cone` and `refusals`; `proofs/last-strict.json` is that same record of a green strict full run plus `tree` and `recordedAt`, and the empty cone's baseline rule refuses a record that is not green, strict and full. Readers read the record, never the transcript. (5) The explanation of the cached-read threshold and the contention factor lives once, in the engine's header; `modules.json`, its template and the READMEs keep their numbers and measurements and point there.

**Consequences.** `proofs.json` roughly doubles in bytes while `claim` is carried beside its parts; that is the price of not breaking the registry, and it ends with the registry change. An adopter's copied engine, refusal tests and templates read stale on the next copy sweep until re-copied. The strict baseline recorded before this change (fe50742, old shape) is replaced by a fresh strict run's record.

## 2026-10-18 — D164: every generated artefact carries one stamp, and the stamp is a content hash, never a version

**Status:** Live

**Recorded by Phase 505. `Fuaran.Core.Idl.Codegen` (`Emit/Core.fs` `Stamp`, `CommentStyle`); rides the `0.39.0` draft (docs/releases/0.39.0.md, Additive). The operator's ruling of 2026-10-17 on the redesign pass's stamp question.**

*Decided: one stamp, keyed by content.* The generator wrote eight hand-spelled header grammars: the F# module named the package VERSION (so a version cut re-stamped every committed generated module with no emission moved, the cost Phase 374's outcome recorded), the TypeScript module and declarations named phase labels frozen at first emission, the three F* targets named a provenance and no version, and the scaffold wrote its own provenance lines. They are now one record (`Stamp`: act, target, disposition, keyed lines) and one renderer (`Stamp.render`, a line-comment or block-comment style). A generated artefact's stamp names the generator's package, never its version; a `vocabulary: sha256:<hex>` line per vocabulary it was generated from, the SHA-256 of that vocabulary's canonical `idl.json` value; and an `emission: sha256:<hex>` line, the SHA-256 of every byte below the stamp.

*Why the emission is hashed rather than an enumerated input set.* The ruling asked for a content hash of the generator's own inputs so that an artefact churns only when its emission changes. The vocabulary is hashed directly, because it is the one input with a canonical form (`Artifact.json`). The others (the kind selection, the module name, the declared support with its verbatim splices, the requested derivations, an F* provenance) have no canonical rendering in this package, and each enters the artefact only through what it makes the generator emit. Hashing the bytes below the stamp therefore covers every one of them, including any added later, without a second canonical form to keep in step, and it makes the stamp checkable from the file alone: an `emission` hash that does not match the bytes below it marks a hand edit.

*Consequences.* (1) A regeneration from unchanged inputs rewrites no byte; a generator release that emits the same bytes leaves every committed artefact untouched. (2) A changed input changes the stamp's hash lines and nothing else in it. A doc-only IDL change moves the `vocabulary` line on every target and the `emission` line only on a target that renders the doc. (3) A property about two emissions (one a prefix of the other, a doc adding only doc lines) is stated below the stamp; the tests read that boundary through one helper (`Snapshots.unstamped`), and `IdlStampTests` holds the stamp itself. (4) The JSON schema keeps no stamp (JSON has no comment syntax and it had no header to unify), and `support.json`'s `version` stays that document's encoding version, which this policy does not govern. (5) A consumer regenerates each committed generated module once on adopting `0.39.0`; after that its drift guard reads only real change.

*Rejected.* Keeping the version (the churn this replaces). A hash of an enumerated input document: a canonical form for `GenSupport` and the derivation requests would be a second encoding of data the emission already carries, and a new input would be silently left out of it until someone remembered to add it.

## 2026-10-18 — D163: a case-name prefix given for a collision is carried onto the wire; no two refusal cases on different seams share a `$type` tag

**Status:** Amended-by D195, D198

**Recorded by Phase 497. `Fuaran.Core.Query` (`QueryErrorWire`, through `QueryCodec`'s error codec);
rides the `0.39.0` draft (docs/releases/0.39.0.md, Breaking).**

*Decided: the tag follows the case name.* D101 qualified `QueryError.QueryPolicyRefused` and
`QueryApprovalRequired` with a `Query…` prefix because `InvokeError.PolicyRefused` and `ApprovalRequired`
are cases in the same namespace, and left the wire tags as they were. The two seams then wrote one
`$type` (`policyRefused`, `approvalRequired`) with the same members, so a refusal document did not say
which seam refused, and each seam's reader accepted the other's: measured before the fix, all four
cross-readings decoded. The rule D101 stated for case names now holds for wire tags: **a refusal case
whose name was prefixed to keep it apart from another seam's case carries the prefix onto the wire**, so
the query seam writes `queryPolicyRefused` / `queryApprovalRequired`, and **no two refusal cases on
different published seams share a `$type` tag.** A new seam refusal is checked against the tags already
on the spine at review, as a new public union is checked against D101.

*Decided: the capability seam keeps its tags.* It is the older seam and the unprefixed case names are
its own; renaming both sides would move every reader for no gain in discrimination.

*Decided: each reader refuses the other seam's tag as an unknown tag.* `UnknownTag` at `$type`, in the
reader's own sentence (`unknown query error: policyRefused`), with no special case naming the other seam:
D99's code and path are the contract, and the sentence is a projection.

*Not done here.* No host encodes either seam's refusal documents and no corpus copy carries them, so no
host expectation or copy fingerprint moved. The seams' refusal codecs as a host-facing corpus family belong
with Phase 528, where those codecs are derived from the IDL; until then the four documents are pinned in
`SeamModelTests`.

## 2026-10-16 — D162: a presence read is not split from a content read — measured, no recorded concurrent fold pairs a reorder or a move with anything; the shape is recorded for the reopening

**Status:** Live

**Decided (Phase 475; the operator's note at accept was "measurement first, and 'not worth the widening' is a
complete outcome", on the pattern of D47).** `Footprint` keeps its six sets. `Ops.footprint`,
`Ops.interference` and `Ops.independent` are unchanged, byte for byte, and so are `proofs/TreeOps.fst`,
`proofs/DagFold.fst`, the oracles, `proofs.json`, `concurrencyLaws` and the `ops/` footprint vectors. No
surface moves and nothing rides a draft.

**D162.1 — what was proposed.** Two reads in `footprint` are not tree facts the script cannot name: a
`ReorderChildren(parent, order)` reads every named child, and a `MoveNode(target, newParent)` reads and
content-writes its target. Each exists so that the op meets a concurrent removal of the node, and each also
makes the op interfere with a concurrent content edit of that node, which it commutes with. Both ops need the
node to EXIST and read nothing of its content. The proposal was a PRESENCE read — satisfied by existence,
written only by a removal — as a slot (`(id, "presence")`, riding Phase 340's sets) or as a new set.

**D162.2 — what it could free, checked in the tree before anything was counted.** Within Core's own ops,
nothing. `RemoveNode`, `MoveNode` and `UpdateNode` all carry an unknown-parent write, and a reorder or a move
carries a structure write, so the unknown-parent clause refuses every such pair whatever the reads say. That
same clause, and not the named-child read, is what makes a reorder meet a concurrent removal of one of its
children in the skeleton algebra. A freeable pair therefore needs a DOMAIN op lowered through
`Footprint.contentEdit`, `slotEdit` or `reading` (none of which records an unknown-parent write) on one side,
and a reorder or a move reaching `Ops.footprint` on the other. That locates the measurement: only a host whose
projection has both shapes can ever be refused by these two reads and nothing else.

**D162.3 — the measurement.** Method: a pair either read could refuse has a reorder-shaped or a move-shaped op
on one side. So, per store, over every lane file:

- **T** — cross-lane op pairs: any two ops in different lane files of one store (an upper bound on
  concurrency; a single-chain file contributes T = 0, a structural zero rather than a finding);
- **Nr / Nm** — reorder-shaped and move-shaped leaf ops, with batches and structural wrappers flattened;
- **R / M** — cross-lane pairs with a reorder (a move) on at least one side, whatever the partner. A partner
  that is not a content edit of the named node is still counted, so both are upper bounds on what the
  widening could free, and a zero is conclusive.

Population: every JSONL file in the maintainers' own working repositories, found by a walk that includes hidden
directories (a first walk that did not missed every store but one, because each keeps its lanes under one). Of 226 files, 112 are live
op-stream ledgers in 30 stores (concurrent write lanes, single-chain bases, frozen predecessor archives), 30 are
committed fixtures, and the rest hold no ops (keys, attestations, evaluation results, prompt packs, work logs).
All 112 parsed, with no unreadable line; one entries ledger with no op lines is named and set aside.

**Result: T = 141,482,012 · Nr = 0 · Nm = 0 · R = 0 · M = 0, over 52,667 leaf ops.** The 30 fixtures (825
ops, T = 12,119) give the same zeros. An independent text search for every reorder and move spelling over all
226 files found 38 occurrences in 9 files, and every one is prose inside a string — a key-file list naming the
`ops/` vectors, a deviations text — never an op kind. The only relocation-shaped ops anywhere are 125
predecessor-model ship ops, all in two frozen single-chain archives (T = 0) whose ops carry no current
footprint (D47).

**The falsifier, stated before the run.** Planted in synthetic two-lane stores: a reorder inside a batch
against a content edit must give R >= 1; a structural move against a payload edit must give M >= 1; the other
direction, an insert against a content edit, must give T = 1 and R = M = 0; a single-lane reorder must be a
structural zero; an unparseable line must be counted, never skipped. All held, and with the reorder spelling
removed from the classifier the first and the fourth went red, so the probe was seen to bite before its zero
was believed.

**D162.4 — why the zero is structural.** The projections of the measured ledgers' hosts are exhaustive matches
with no reorder and no move arm: their ops lower to inserts, removes, whole-node and slot edits, reads, and the
empty footprint. The hosts whose projections DO reach Core's reorder and move arms pass skeleton ops through
`Ops.footprint` beside their own `contentEdit`-shaped payload edits — exactly the pair the widening frees — and
none has recorded a multi-lane ledger: the one such ledger committed is a single-lane conformance fixture of
three ops.

**D162.5 — the demand, which is not the measurement, and the reopening.** fuaran#2293's experiment, over one UI
consumer's generated triads (18,597), found 1,629 of 3,791 footprint-refused-but-commuting pairs to be a reorder
against a restyle or kind edit of a named child, and 354 of 1,820 a move against an edit of the moved node once
that consumer's projection was slot-precise. Those are a generator's pairs, not recorded folds, and are kept
here as the reason to reopen rather than as the count. **Reopen on the first recorded multi-lane ledger of a
host whose projection reaches the reorder or move arm beside a `contentEdit`- or `slotEdit`-shaped op** — the
UI op-stream DAG, once fuaran#2293 puts it on Core, is the expected one. Re-measuring is the census above over
that ledger's lanes, with its falsifier.

**D162.6 — the shape, for whoever reopens it (an analysis of the clauses as written, not a proof).** The two
shapes do not free the same pairs:

- **A slot.** Replacing the read of `x` with a slot read `(x, "presence")` frees a SLOT edit of `x` (no slot
  clashes, and `slotsAgainstNode` sees no whole-node access of `x`), but not a `contentEdit x`: a slot read of
  `x` meets a whole-node content write of `x` by the existing `LeftSlotsRightNode` clause. That is also why it
  is sound with no new obligation: a domain that lowers a DESTROY through `contentEdit` (one measured host's
  bundle retirement does) still meets the reorder. No record change.
- **A set.** A new presence set can free a `contentEdit` partner too, but only if every op that can make a
  node absent writes its presence. A projection that lowers a destroy through `contentEdit` would then make a
  freed reorder unsound for it, so the widening would bind every projection, not Core alone, and the record
  change is mirrored by hand in `proofs/DagFold.fst` and a second repository's proof tree (D47).

The consumer evidence above was measured slot-precise for the move, which is the slot shape's case. So a
reopening should start from the slot, and take the set only on a recorded count of `contentEdit` partners.

**Rejected: build it now, because the UI DAG is ruled onto Core.** The ruling makes the demand likely; it does
not make it recorded. Building to a generator's count before one recorded ledger exists ships a lemma, an
oracle differential, a law-family draw and a verdict change for every plane that reads `independent`, to free a
set measured at zero. The slot shape needs no record change, so waiting costs the reopening little.

**Not added: an assertion to catch the world changing back.** The change that reopens this is a new host's
ledger, which nothing in this repository reads, so no test here can see it; the trigger is stated in D162.5
instead.

## 2026-10-16 — D161: `Column.ofCells` has no boxed path — an `Int` under a float or a decimal column is already the float or the decimal of its value on its only path, and a cell the type does not carry is refused, so Phase 472's Core half is a finding and not a change; the matching compute decision is `Fuaran.Core.Compute` D40

**Status:** Live

**Phase 472 asked Core to widen an `Int` under a `Float` or `Decimal` column "on the boxed path, as on the
typed one". The premise is false, and no code moves; this entry records why, so the question is not
re-opened.**

**Context.** The compute repository's `Vec.packAt` packs a column typed when every present cell is one the
type carries and BOXES it — every cell as it was — otherwise, so until compute's Phase 472 an int under a
float column read as its float on one carrier and as an int on the other, and one unrelated row decided
which (compute `DECISIONS.md` D38 item 5). Phase 472 widens the int on the boxed form too, in both
repositories; this is Core's half.

**Decision.**

1. **Core has no boxed path.** `ColumnData` is seven typed cases (`Ints`, `Floats`, `Bools`, `Strs`,
   `Dates`, `Timestamps`, `Decimals`) and nothing else; there is no `Cell list` carrier and no boxed
   fall-back anywhere in `Fuaran.Core.Column`. `Column.ofCells` (`storageOfCells`) is the one
   construction that reads cells: under `FloatType` it holds an `Int i` as `float i`, under `DecimalType`
   as `string i`, and REFUSES the first present cell whose type does not widen into the column's
   (`TypeMismatch`, naming the cell's type) rather than falling back to anything. Since `1.0.0` (Phase
   423) a Core column therefore reads an int under a float column as its float, whatever stands beside it;
   the suite pins it (`ColumnTests`: "ofCells normalises a widened Int: Float in a float column, Decimal in
   a decimal column" — `Column.toCells` answers `Float 1.0` for `Int 1`, `Decimal "1"` for `Int 1`, and the
   column equals the one built from the normal cells). A go-red test for the shard's ask cannot be
   written, because there is nothing red to show; the pinning test above is the assertion that goes red
   if this ever changes back.

2. **No caller reads an `Int` back out of a float or decimal column, because none can.** `Column.cell`
   on `Floats` answers `Float`, on `Decimals` `Decimal`; `tryFloats` / `tryDecimals` lend the typed vector.
   The survey the phase asked for reduces to that fact: a downstream consumer of Core can only ever have
   seen the widened cell. The compute repository's boxed vector was the one place an `Int` survived under
   a float or decimal type, and a boxed vector handed to `Column.ofCells` (through compute's
   `Vec.toColumn`) was widened here on the way in — which is why compute's half needs no Core change and
   no pin raise: compute pins the public `0.37.0`, and Core's open draft (`0.38.0` at the take, `0.38.1`
   at the landing) is untouched by this phase.

3. **Nothing rides the draft.** No source, test, api baseline or stability record of this repository
   moves; the open draft's release record gains no entry, because there is no behaviour to record. This decision
   is the whole of Core's half.

**Consequences.** Cell-locality of a column's reading holds in Core by construction and, since compute's
Phase 472, in the compute repository's `Vec.packAt` on both carriers; a reader of either repository
meets the same cell for the same input. Compute's D40 records the other half and closes its D38 item 5.

## 2026-10-15 — D160: every checked op-stream writer checks every member a line carries, the strings it quotes itself as well as the span it embeds, so no checked writer returns text the strict reader refuses; closes D158.6

**Status:** Live

**Phase 473, the model first: `proofs/OpStreamLoad.fst`'s writer moved, re-verified with the pinned prover and
re-extracted before the writers did. Rides the `0.38.0` draft (`docs/releases/0.38.0.md`).**

**D160.1 — the gap.** D158.6 recorded it: the checked writers (Phase 301) held only the span they EMBED to
`checkRaw`. The strings they quote themselves go through `JsonString.quote`, which escapes every control (Phase
287) but writes a surrogate as it finds it, so after Phase 466 an unpaired surrogate in one of them was written
`Ok` and refused by the reader. The survey of what each writer quotes: a record's `actor` object, `prevHash`
and `hash`; a capture's `eff`, `det`, `prevHash` and `hash`; a snapshot's `prevHash` and `hash`; a DAG node's
`id`, `parents` and `actor`. Two further writers quote strings and are covered already, because their output
is an op ENCODING a record embeds and `checkRaw` reads: `Attributed.encodeEnvelope` and the keyed capture
encoding. `seq` and `occ` are numerals the writer spells and cannot be unreadable.

**D160.2 — one checker, every member, line order.** `checkedLines` takes the members each line carries as
`(member, text)` in line order, the embedded span among them, and refuses the first that `checkRaw` refuses —
the SAME function the reader's grammar is applied through, rather than a second surrogate test that could drift
from it. The refusal is `JsonlWriteFault { Line; Member; Reason = Unreadable(LoneSurrogate path) }`, naming the
member (`actor`, `prevHash`, …) and, inside it, the path (`$["id"]`). No new `JsonlWriteFaultReason` case: the
existing `Unreadable` already says "the reader would refuse this", which is exactly the claim. `Dag.tryToJsonl`
checks its four members the same way. On `Ok` every writer's text is the unchecked writer's, byte for byte.

**D160.3 — the model, and what its premise still owes.** `checked_lines` checks `record_members` (actor object,
op span, `prevHash`, `hash`) and the round trip is re-proved over it. Its `records_wf` premise is NOT retired:
the READABILITY half of `wf_str` is now enforced by the writer, but the premise's other half is the model's
alphabet bridge — a host hands the writer each string spelled as the escapes the writer emits — which no check
on the written text can establish (an escaped high half before a raw low one reads, and is still not a canonical
spelling). The premise's comment says so. A twin pins the write-side refusal, and the oracle differential
compares it against production over records whose actor, `prevHash` and `hash` carry an unpaired surrogate.

**D160.4 — the version.** A checked writer that returned `Ok` now refuses (behavioural); no public signature
moves (`checkedLines` and `firstUnreadable` are internal). The standing `0.38.0` draft already carries the
breaking class, so the change RIDES it.

## 2026-10-15 — D159: Core's parser takes a limits record and enforces it on the way down, so a wire host bounds the parse through Core alone; Core still states no limit values and is not a section-21 host; a breach is a typed outcome and never malformed JSON; D84's "no shared limits-taking entry point" clause is refined

**Status:** Amended-by D183

**Recorded by Phase 465. ADDITIVE, riding the `0.38.0` draft (`docs/releases/0.38.0.md`).
`proofs/JsonParse.fst` (and its extracted oracle), `proofs/Limits.fst`, `src/Fuaran.Core.Wire/Json.fs`,
`DecodeError.fs`, `Decoder.fs`, `conformance/decode/`, `docs/conformance-corpus.md` ("The limits"),
`proofs.json`. Requirement `suggest-2026-10-15-core-json-syntax-and-rust-spine`, clause S3.**

**D159.1 — the ruling, and what it refines.** The operator ruled on 2026-10-15, refining D84: *"Core is
still NOT a section-21 host and states no limit VALUES; it gains only the MECHANISM, a parse entry point
taking a limits record enforced on the way down."* D84's ruling (b) stands in every clause but one: the
limit values, their units and the error envelope belong to each wire specification, Core's 512 nesting
cap is its own stack guard and not a conformance claim, and `proofs/Limits.fst` keeps the UI wire's
values as named premises. The clause this entry refines is D84's last sentence — *"No shared
limits-taking entry point is added: the hosts already carry the enforcement, in the units and with the
error the section requires."* That sentence was written against the state in which every wire host
carried its own parser. Phase 462 made Core the single owner of the JSON-syntax layer (D157), and the
UI wire's section 21.2 rule 4 requires a limit to be enforced ON THE WAY DOWN, during the parse: a host
that parses with Core and measures the tree afterwards has already paid the cost the limit exists to
refuse, so without a limits-taking entry point every host that needs limits keeps a parser of its own,
and two parsers drift — which is the defect D157 closed. So the mechanism is Core's and the values are
not: `Json.parseWithLimits policy limits input` takes a `JsonLimits` record, a wire host passes its own
specification's numbers, and nothing in Core names a number, a unit's conformance status, or a wire's
error code.

**D159.2 — the record, and what each bound counts.** `JsonLimits` carries five bounds: `MaxDepth` (nested
objects and arrays admitted, the root counting as one — the cap every entry point already had),
`MaxStringLength` (Unicode code points in ONE decoded string or member key, a surrogate pair counting as
one, whichever spelling each unit arrived in), `MaxArrayLength` (items in one array), `MaxObjectMembers`
(members in one object — an erased member null is not a member, so the tolerant read stays the strict
read of the erased document under a bound), and `MaxDocumentBytes` (UTF-8 bytes of the whole input,
counted off its UTF-16 units; a native length under-counts a CJK document threefold). Items and members
are two fields and not one, though the UI wire's section 21.1 states one value for both: the breach
names the bound it passed, and a member-count breach reported as an array-length breach sends an author
to repair the wrong thing — the diagnosis that section's own prose forbids for the two depth bounds.
`JsonLimits.depthOnly maxDepth` is the record every pre-existing entry point runs under: the three
counts can never reach `Int32.MaxValue`, so under it no breach but the depth cap's can arise, and
`parse`, `parseDetailed*`, the tolerant reads, `Decoder.parse*` and `Json.Reader.read` answer every
document exactly as before — the 512-deep stack guard and no size limit.

**D159.3 — on the way down, and where each breach is raised.** The byte bound is one comparison before a
character is read (the count is made only when the input's UTF-16 length could encode past the bound).
The depth cap is tested at the bracket, as it always was. The items bound is tested at the array loop's
head, before `item` is called, so the `max + 1`-th item is refused where it would start and no character
of it is read; the members bound after the loop's whitespace and before the key, at the key's opening
quote; the string bound inside the string reader's unit check, after the two surrogate tests and before
the unit is appended — on the escape-free fast path the count runs during the scan, before the one
`Substring` that builds the string, so a hostile string is refused before it is assembled. The first
fault in document order wins, whichever kind it is: a breach outranks malformed text after it, and
malformed text outranks a breach after it.

**D159.4 — the breach is typed, carries the path, and never echoes the input.** `JsonRefusal` is the
limited parse's refusal: `Malformed of JsonError` (exactly `parseDetailed`'s refusal, kind, message and
position) or `LimitExceeded of JsonLimitBreach` — the `JsonLimit`, its `Declared` value, the `Path` to
the container the breach was raised in (the array whose count passed the bound, the object whose count
or whose key's length did, the container opened at the depth bound; a string value's own path; the root
for document bytes) and the `Position`. `JsonErrorKind` gains NO case: a breach is not a parse error, a
thirteen-case match stays exhaustive, and `DecodeError.ofJsonRefusal` maps the breach to
`DecodeCode.LimitExceeded` AT ITS PATH with a sentence naming the limit and the declared value
(`limit arrayLength of 2 exceeded`), never to `InvalidJson`. `Decoder.parseWithLimits` is the typed-decode
form of the same call. The scanner tracks the path as two parallel lists, a frame per open container
(the member key being read, the item index being read), so a member costs no allocation and an unfilled
slot ends the path at the container. `PathSegment` moves from `DecodePath.fs` to `Json.fs` to sit below
the parser that now reports it; its full name is unchanged.

**D159.5 — the model first, and what is proved.** `proofs/JsonParse.fst`'s descent takes a `lims` record
(three bounds, each `Unbounded` or a budget spent as the depth cap is) and the entry point
`parse_limited` takes a byte verdict as a parameter, as the float readback is. The descent carries the
breach internally as an `ekind` case `LimitExceeded`, confined by the return types (`bounds_confined`)
to a bound that is actually set — so `parse`, at `unbounded`, is seen by the type-checker to keep its
thirteen kinds — and `parse_limited` lifts every breach, the depth cap's `MaxDepthExceeded` included, to
the distinct `RLimit` constructor. Proved: `limited_at_no_bound_is_the_parser` (at no bound the limited
entry point answers exactly what `parse` answers, the depth cap lifted), `limit_never_reported_as_malformed`
(a `RErr` of the limited parse carries one of the thirteen kinds), `bytes_checked_before_the_descent`,
`string_bound_exact` and `items_bound_exact` (on the canonical string and array families each bound is
exact at every length and every bound — accepted at the bound, refused one past it, with the bound's own
breach); exhibited: the members bound from both sides, the depth lift, a breach outranking a later
malformed item, the string bound reaching a member key, the byte verdict first (`limits_exhibited`).
Every pre-existing theorem is restated over the generalised descent and still holds; the null-absorption
bridge (Phase 190) is stated at no bound, and section 11's run lemmas say so. The differential compares
`Json.parseWithLimits` with the extracted `parse_limited` over hand-picked documents, the near-miss
table and a bounded soup under five records, with the platform's UTF-8 encoder as the byte verdict's
independent oracle, and a go-red case (a model handed a wider items bound accepts what production
refuses). NOT modelled: the breach's path (the decode vectors pin it) and the byte count itself.

**D159.6 — the vectors, and what a host owes.** The `decode/` family gains one vector per bound at the
bound (accepted) and one past it (`LimitExceeded` at the pinned path), the astral and the CJK vectors
beside them so a host counting UTF-16 units or bytes fails by name, a key-length vector, two nested-path
vectors, and the two first-fault-wins vectors. Each declares the record it runs under as a `limits`
member (`depth`, `stringLength`, `arrayLength`, `objectMembers`, `documentBytes`); a vector without one
runs at the parser's own cap. A host that parses through Core certifies by reproducing every code and
path; a host carrying a reader of its own (the IDL host's generated readers do, at the parser's own cap)
excludes the family's limits vectors by name and says why, as `DecodeVectorsIdl.exclusion` does.

**Rejected.** (1) A `LimitExceeded` case on `JsonErrorKind`: it would break every exhaustive match for a
fact no `JsonError` consumer branches on, and it would carry the limit, the value and the path in a record
built for a position and a sentence. (2) Measuring after the parse (`Json.firstRepeatedMember`'s shape):
it cannot satisfy enforcement on the way down, which is the whole reason the mechanism exists. (3) One
field for items and members, as the UI wire's table has it: see D159.2. (4) Modelling the path in F\*:
it would thread a path accumulator through every parser and every induction for a property the vectors
pin exactly; the model carries the suffix, as it does for every refusal.
## 2026-10-15 — D158: the op-stream JSONL reader reads by the strict grammar at every depth; a repeated key, a raw control and a raw unpaired surrogate are refused at the path they are at; a container value is walked by its grammar; the reader shares D157's vectors, not its code

**Status:** Amended-by D199

**Phase 466, the model first: `proofs/OpStreamLoad.fst` (the scanner's accept set) moved, re-verified with the
pinned prover and re-extracted before `Jsonl.fs` did. Requirement `suggest-2026-10-15-core-json-syntax-and-rust-spine`,
clause S4 (operator ruling 2026-10-15). Rides the `0.38.0` draft (`docs/releases/0.38.0.md`).**

**D158.1 — the committed stores first.** Before the reader changed, every committed `.json` and `.jsonl`
document in the workspace was scanned under the stricter rules, read-only, at each repository's `HEAD`
(`git show`, so no working tree counts): a repeated member name at any depth (compared after unescaping),
a raw U+0000 to U+001F inside a string, and a string that is not well-formed UTF-16 (escaped or raw).
Ninety-nine repositories: 29,089 `.json` documents and 127 `.jsonl` files (67,279 lines), the 73 op-stream
lane files among them (17,177 lines). **No `.jsonl` line breaks a rule — no op-stream line, and no line of any
other store.** Seventeen `.json` documents do, and every one is a deliberate fixture: the five JSON reject
vectors of the UI wire's conformance corpus (`reject-json-duplicate-key`, the two lone surrogates, the raw
control, the split surrogate pair) in its three copies, and the two copies of a renderer test's
`synthetic-escaping.json`, whose lone surrogate is the input it exists to escape. None is read by this reader.
Phase 462's scan (D157.8) was the same method over a narrower set; this one read every repository's committed
tree.

**D158.2 — what the reader refuses now.** `OpStream.Jsonl` is Core's second JSON reader, kept free of a
`Fuaran.Core.Wire` reference by D2. Phase 462's worker found it kept the FIRST value of a repeated top-level
key (Phase 45) and passed raw controls and raw lone surrogates through. It now refuses, with three new
`JsonlFaultReason` cases appended after every existing one (so each existing case keeps its tag), each
naming a path spelled as `DecodePath.render` spells one (`$["op"]["items"][1]["id"]`):

- **`RepeatedKey path`** — a key read twice in one object, at ANY depth, compared after unescaping. Refused
  at the repeated key's opening quote once its value is read, so a refusal inside the value wins: the order
  `Wire.Json` reads in (D157.2). The path is the repeated member's.
- **`RawControl path`** — a raw U+0000 to U+001F inside a string, at the character. The path is the member
  or item the string is in; for a key, the object that holds it (its own name is not yet read).
- **`LoneSurrogate path`** — a RAW surrogate unit that is not half of a pair, at the unit. A raw high unit is
  judged once what follows it is known: the end of the line is the token's `UnterminatedString`, a raw control
  is its own refusal and an escape the grammar does not have is that escape's.

An unpaired surrogate ESCAPE keeps the answer it always had (`InvalidEscape` of the escape's text at its
backslash, six characters or twelve), so no line refused before is refused differently for it. **A pair split
between the two spellings now READS** — an escaped high half before a raw low one, or a raw high half before an
escaped low one — where the reader refused it: that is Phase 299's rule (well-formed UTF-16, whichever
spelling each unit arrived in), which `Wire.Json` already held. It is the one place the change admits a line
it refused, and it admits exactly the lines the grammar does.

**D158.3 — a container value is walked by its grammar.** Until now an array or object VALUE was balanced and
its strings checked, and the rest of its grammar was the decoder's. A repeated key inside a value cannot be
found without reading the value's keys, and the strict grammar's vectors include values the balanced walk
read (`[00]`, `[1,NaN]`), so `skipValue` now reads every depth: members, items, separators, literals.
`ExpectedCommaOrBracket` is new for an array's separator. A line ending inside a value is still
`UnterminatedContainer` at the OUTERMOST opening, where the balanced walk refused it. The walk keeps an explicit
stack of open containers, so no depth of nesting exhausts the call stack (the model's recursion is that
stack). Every reader built on the scanner inherits it: `fromJsonl*`, `Snapshots.ofJsonl`, `captureFromJsonl`,
`Attributed.decodeEnvelope`, `Dag.fromJsonl`, and `checkRaw` under every checked writer.

**D158.4 — the model.** `string_tail` gains the path and the three string rules; `skip_val` / `obj_members` /
`arr_items` replace the balanced `skip_container`; `members_loop` refuses a repeated key where `first_wins`
dropped it. All three Phase-454 theorems are re-proved: totality by typing, faults locate (a new refusal's
position is within its line like every other), and the round trip, whose premise `wf_str` now also excludes a
raw control and an unpaired surrogate. That narrowing is the change itself: a record carrying such a string
is not one a reader of the strict grammar reads back. Six twins pin the new answers. One boundary is new and
recorded in the model's header: the model compares keys by their SPELLING (it has no code units), production
after unescaping, so the two agree wherever keys are spelled without escapes, which the differential's
generators keep.

**D158.5 — certified against the grammar's vectors.** `JsonlStrictGrammar` reads every vector of the
`refusals/` family that applies to a line twice — as a member's value, and as the line itself when it is an
object — and holds the line reader to the grammar's verdict in the matching class (`DuplicateMember` →
`RepeatedKey`; `BadEscape` → `RawControl`, `InvalidEscape` or `LoneSurrogate`; `MalformedNumber` and
`UnexpectedChar` → `InvalidLiteral`; `TrailingCharacters` → `ExpectedCommaOrBrace` or `TrailingContent`).
Column vectors the column codec refuses over well-formed JSON must READ at the line. **Two classes do not
apply, named in the suite rather than skipped:** `overflowing-exponent` (`1e999`), a value-domain refusal
(Core's value model has no non-finite float, D157.2) where the line grammar reads a number token and hands the
span to its decoder; and every wire-profile vector, which is not JSON text. The cases a JSON file cannot spell
(a raw lone surrogate) are pinned beside them, with positions and paths.

**D158.6 — the writers are not changed here, and that is a finding routed on, not an omission.** The checked
writers (`tryToJsonl`, `tryCaptureToJsonl`, `Snapshots.tryToJsonl`, `Dag.tryToJsonl`) check the embedded span
(`checkRaw`, now strict). The strings they spell themselves — an actor's fields, `prevHash`, `hash`, a capture's
`eff` and `det` — are quoted by `JsonString.quote`, which escapes every control, so only an UNPAIRED SURROGATE
in one of them can reach a line the reader now refuses. Before this phase such a record was written and read
back (and hashed with the platform's U+FFFD, `sha256Hash`'s note). Three of the four writers live outside this
phase's files, so the fix — every checked writer refusing a string a reader of the grammar cannot read back,
by member — is a successor's, filed as its own phase from this one's outcome.

**D158.7 — the version.** `JsonlFaultReason` gains four cases (`union-widening`, breaking: an exhaustive match
gains arms) and a published reader refuses lines it read. The standing `0.38.0` draft already carries the
breaking class (D157.9), so the change RIDES it; the API baseline `api/Fuaran.Core.OpStream.txt` moves by the
four cases. The ledger cut and the cohort raise are the slot's, not this phase's.

## 2026-10-15 — D157: Core owns the JSON-syntax layer every Fuaran wire cites; a repeated member name and a raw control inside a string are refused at every decode entry point, the model first; an erased member null is not an occurrence; first-wins (D113) is superseded; a value with a repeated member has no rendering a guarded renderer gives

**Status:** Live

**Recorded by Phase 462. `proofs/JsonParse.fst` and `proofs/WireCanon.fst` (and their extracted oracles),
`src/Fuaran.Core.Wire/Json.fs`, `Canon.fs`, `Corpus.fs`, `src/Fuaran.Core.Idl.Codegen/Emit/TypeScriptCodec.fs`,
`conformance/refusals/`, `conformance/decode/`, `docs/conformance-corpus.md` ("The JSON-syntax layer"),
`proofs.json`; rides the `0.38.0` draft (`docs/releases/0.38.0.md`). Requirement
`suggest-2026-10-15-core-json-syntax-and-rust-spine`, clause S1.**

**D157.1 — the single-owner ruling.** Every Fuaran wire shares one JSON layer below its own vocabulary, and
each specification either restated its rules or omitted them: the UI wire's section 20 rows and section 21
limits, the model-execution wire's duplicate-member rule, the program wire's silence. The UI wire records
why that is a defect rather than a style (its 20.1: the reference host carried two parsers with two accept
sets, and the gap closes when they are one parser). Core is now the single owner of the syntax layer:
`docs/conformance-corpus.md` states the rows, the refusal classes and the entry points they bind as a
citable normative section, the `refusals/` family carries one vector per row and per boundary acceptance,
and the `decode/` family carries each row at the shape reader. A wire specification cites the section and
restates nothing. The limit VALUES are not here: D84 stands, Core is not a section-21 host, and Phase 465
adds the limits MECHANISM (a parse taking a limits record) while each wire keeps its own values, units and
envelope. A stricter host-operational ceiling is deployment policy, never a conformance claim.

**D157.2 — what the parser refuses now, and where.** Two inputs the one scanner accepted:

- **A repeated member name in one object** — `JsonErrorKind.DuplicateMember`, a new thirteenth case, at the
  repeated name's opening quote, message `repeated member name in one object`. The check runs when the
  member is ACCUMULATED, after its value is read: a refusal inside the value still wins, and under the strict
  policy a repeated member whose value is `null` is the null's refusal. Names are compared after unescaping
  (`{"a":1,"a":2}` is a repeat); the same name in two sibling objects or at two depths is not; case
  differs.
- **A raw C0 control (U+0000 to U+001F) inside a string** — `BadEscape`, at the character, message
  `unescaped control character U+00XX in a string`, before the surrogate test. Phase 299's precedent is
  followed: `BadEscape` already names "this string's content is not well-formed", and a fourteenth kind would
  cost every exhaustive match for no decision a caller takes.

Both ride the one scanner (Phase 368), so every entry point answers alike: `parse*`, `parseDetailed*`, the
tolerant reads, `Decode.parse*`, `Decoder.parse*`, `Json.Reader.read`, and everything above them. A test
holds every entry point to one answer per vector. Rows 2, 3, 4 and 6 of the UI wire's section 20.2 (content
after the root, the number grammar, a bare non-finite literal, an unpaired surrogate) were already refused
everywhere. Row 7 (`1e999`) stays refused: Core's value model has no non-finite float, so the refusal is the
value domain's, not the syntax's; a wire that admits a non-finite number at its syntax layer says so as its
one divergence.

**D157.3 — an erased member null is not an occurrence.** Under `EraseMemberNull`, `{"a":null,"a":1}` reads
as `{"a":1}` and `{"a":1,"a":null}` reads as `{"a":1}` too. The alternative (count the erased member) would
falsify Phase 190's proved bridge — the tolerant read IS the strict read of the document with its member
nulls deleted — and the deletion leaves no name behind to repeat. The accumulator is the set, and an erased
member is never accumulated. `null_absorption_is_erasure` and `policies_agree_off_the_fork` both still hold,
which is why the check sits after the value rather than before it: with the check first, strict refused
`{"a":1,"a":null}` as a duplicate and the tolerant read accepted it, and the two theorems could not both be
true.

**D157.4 — D113's first-wins is superseded.** D113.3 made the three hosts agree by keeping a repeated key's
first value. Refusal makes them agree as well and closes the smuggling case the UI wire's 20.3 names, which
is the differential the device demo is built to show (`langsec-microcontroller-demo.md`, L1). The generated
TypeScript reader (`dParse`, the F# reader's twin) refuses the same two inputs with the same messages; the
pinned corners read `InvalidJson` at the root on all three hosts; the mutation law draws the corner and
holds the hosts to one answer. First-wins remains only where no text exists: `dMap` and the F# host's map
over a value handed in keep the first entry, as D113.3 said, and nothing reaches them from text with a
repeated key.

**D157.5 — the encoder side.** `JObj` admits a repeated key, so `Json.render` and `Canon.render` could write
text the parser now refuses, and the admission test the UI wire's 20.2 states ("no conformant encoder can
reach it") did not hold of Core itself. `Json.firstRepeatedMember` finds the first object carrying a name
twice, in document order, and the three guarded renderers (`Json.tryRender`, `Canon.tryRender`, and
`Canonical.tryWrite` since Phase 495, which this ruling first missed) refuse on it after
the non-finite float and the ill-formed string. The total renderers stay total: a repeated key does not make
a digest platform-dependent, so D84's rule (refuse where a digest depends on it) does not apply, and the chain
pre-images are unchanged. The fuzz law (`Corpus.fuzzRoundTrip`) keeps drawing keys with replacement and
holds the refusal as the law where a value repeats one.

**D157.6 — the models moved first.** `proofs/JsonParse.fst` gains `CCtrl` (a raw control, spelt by the
bridge), `DuplicateMember`, `has_key` over the accumulated members, the refusal arms, a thirteenth
reachability witness and `raw_control_refused` / `repeated_member_refused`; the surrogate well-formedness
lemmas and the null-absorption bridge are re-proved over the new grammar. `proofs/WireCanon.fst`'s bridge to
the parser (section 14) carries one new hypothesis, `distinct_keys` — section 6's reader reads exactly what
`render` emits, repeated keys included, and the parser no longer does — preserved by the sort and threaded
through the member induction (`keys_apart`); `pc` sends a `CPlain` carrying a whitespace control to `COther`,
the same boundary a surrogate sits at. The oracles are re-extracted and the differentials run over the new
alphabet (a raw tab is in the soup).

**D157.7 — the layer checks pre-empted on text.** `ColumnCodec.decode` and `QueryCodec.decodeArgs` refuse a
repeated key before their own duplicate checks run; those checks still answer a value built in memory, and
their tests now exercise both routes.

**D157.8 — the committed stores.** Every committed `.json` and `.jsonl` document in this repository and in the
workspace's nine roadmap stores was scanned for a repeated member name and a raw control before this landed:
none was found (the scan and its count are in the phase's outcome). The op-stream JSONL scanner itself is
Phase 466's: it still keeps the first of a repeated key and passes a raw control, and it has no Wire
dependency to share the grammar through.

**D157.9 — the version.** `JsonErrorKind` gains a case (`union-widening`, breaking: every exhaustive match in
a consumer moves) and a published reader refuses documents it accepted. The standing `0.38.0` draft already
carries the breaking class, so the change RIDES it rather than advancing it; the cohort is raised when the
slot is cut.

## 2026-10-14 — D156: the two slowest proof modules spend their time in a handful of queries whose context carries definitions the proof never needs; the cost is cut by naming what each query may use, not by weakening any statement

**Status:** Amended-by D197

**Recorded by Phase 458. `proofs/Temporal.fst`, `proofs/OpStreamLoad.fst`, `proofs/modules.json`,
`proofs/README.md`. No production code, no theorem statement and no extracted oracle changed.**

**D156.1 — the profile, taken before anything changed.** Each module was checked cold, at the leg's flags
(`--z3rlimit 40 --quake 3 --report_assumes error`) plus `--timing --query_stats`, by the pinned prover invoked
directly on the file, its dependencies already in the cache, with no other prover on the machine.

- **`Temporal`: 1,928s.** Two declarations took 85% of it. `year_ends_ok_at` took 1,073s. One goal took
  135s, 153s and 785s on the three quake seeds: the precondition `yoe < k - 1` of the recursive call, a linear
  fact. It used at most 5.9 units of a 40-unit rlimit, so the rlimit does not meter the time and does not bound
  it. The time goes into arithmetic over `year_ends_ok`'s unfolded body, which carries nested integer
  divisions. `days_of_civil_mono` took 565s, with its one ensures goal at 484s, 67s and 13s. Every other
  declaration was under 60s: `cmp_prefix` 56s, `doe_in_year` 38s, `yoe_recovered` 32s, `instant_text_parts`
  31s, `days_civil_days` 23s, and about two hundred small queries after them. The normalisation of the 800
  year ends (`year_ends_computed`) took 0.2s. The Phase 430 note's account was that the normalisation took
  close to three minutes, and that is not where the time goes. The 576s that Phase 430 recorded was one
  lucky draw from the same distribution.
- **`OpStreamLoad`: 413s, 367s of it in the solver.** `actor_field_reads` took 158s (40 goals per seed at
  `--fuel 10 --z3rlimit 160`, the heaviest 7-13s each) and `line_members` took 106s. Next came
  `string_tail_ext` 24s, `clean_quote` 20s, `string_tail_quoted` 13s and `skip_value_actor` 9s. Unlike
  `Temporal`, these costs are steady across seeds. The fuel unfolds character-level recursions the two
  lemmas only reach through lemma calls: `olit` over the concrete keys, `string_tail`, `skip_value`,
  `quote_body` and `app` over symbolic strings.

**D156.2 — the lever is the query's context, applied lemma by lemma, one change per measured run.** Each
lever below was first measured on its own declaration (`--admit_except`, three or six quake seeds), then on
the whole module.

- `year_ends_ok_at`: at `--fuel 1 --ifuel 0` alone the goal still took 12s to 224s over six seeds, so that
  lever **did not pay** and was reverted. What paid was a split. `year_ends_ok_head` and `year_ends_ok_tail`
  each unfold `year_ends_ok` once, the walk calls them at `--fuel 0`, and every query is under a second.
- `days_of_civil_mono`: the one-year case moved to `doy_mono`. That alone left the ensures goal at 5-68s
  per seed. `--fuel 0 --ifuel 0` brought it to 6-49s. A `--using_facts_from` that drops `days_of_civil`,
  `year_start`, `year_base`, `era_of`, `yoe_of`, `month_start`, `mp_of_month`, `year_len`, `shifted_leap`,
  `g`, `days_in` and `is_leap` brought every goal under a second, because every fact the lemma uses
  already arrives through a lemma call. `yoe_recovered` follows the same pattern: it now states its two
  division steps (`lemma_div_le`) and runs without `g`'s body. `doe_in_year` and `cmp_prefix` only needed
  `--fuel 0 --ifuel 0`.
- `actor_field_reads` and `line_members`: lowering the fuel to the member lists' length (`--fuel 5` /
  `--fuel 6`) took 156s of solver time to 109s. A `--using_facts_from` without `olit`, `string_tail`,
  `skip_value`, `skip_container`, `quote_body` and `JsonParse.app` took it to 29s, and `line_members` to 18s.
  The scoped `--z3rlimit 160` came out, because neither lemma uses more than 11 units of the leg's 40.
  `string_tail_quoted` and `clean_quote` lost a third of their time at `--ifuel 1`.

**D156.3 — the levers that did not pay, measured.** `--ext context_pruning` on `OpStreamLoad`:
`actor_field_reads` spent 146s in the solver against 156s, inside the noise, so it was not adopted.
`--fuel 4` on `actor_field_reads` refuted two goals and spent 372s. `--ifuel 1` on `string_tail_ext`
refuted a goal. `instant_text_parts` (31s) refuted three goals at `--fuel 0 --ifuel 0`, and at
`--fuel 1 --ifuel 1` it ran past 600s and was killed. All four were reverted. **No module was split.** Once
the context was right, neither module had a section left whose cost would justify a separately checked
module and the oracle, ladder and test renames a split carries.

**D156.4 — the result, from cold observations interleaved before and after on one machine.** All runs used
the same direct invocation as D156.1, with no other prover on the machine. `OpStreamLoad`: 413s, 426s and
411s before; 203s, 195s and 194s after. `Temporal`: 1,928s and 1,924s before; 164s, 163s and 169s after.
The proof leg's own `-Extract` run over both cones measured 182s and 295s on a machine that other work held
at 60-70% CPU. Its fresh extraction matched every committed oracle byte for byte, because each new lemma is
`noextract`. `modules.json` re-seeds both budgets from the slowest of those observations by its own rule
(`Temporal` 370s, `OpStreamLoad` 590s). Every theorem's statement is unchanged. Each module's header and
`proofs/README.md` say how to keep a new lemma cheap: name the facts it uses.

## 2026-10-14 — D155: the lane DAG's remaining boundaries are modelled in a sibling module; the index is proved under a stated slot-agreement reading, and `cut`'s band is kept though the replay contract does not need it

**Status:** Amended-by D197

**Recorded by Phase 457. `proofs/DagPrimitives.fst` (new, opens `DagFold`), `proofs/oracle/DagPrimitives.fs`,
`proofs.json`, `proofs/coverage-exclusions.json`, `proofs/check.ps1`, `proofs/modules.json`. No production
code changed: no defect was found, so `DagOpStream.fs` and its API baseline are untouched and nothing rides the
`0.38.0` draft.**

**D155.1 — a sibling module rather than a fifth section of `DagFold.fst`.** The new sections are about 1,300
lines. `DagFold` was already one of the leg's slowest modules (117s cold under `--quake 3`, against a 360s
budget), and the new proofs only use its lemmas, so nothing in it had to change. `DagPrimitives` opens it, checks in about 25s,
and is registered, extracted and twinned like every other model. DagFold's own budget did not move.

**D155.2 — the index is proved under a slot-agreement reading, and that reading is named rather than
proved.** Each of `Reach.mergeBase`, `commonBase`, `between` and `tryTopoOrder` is modelled over section 20's
slots and proved to answer what the DAG-level function answers. The model reads a slot's bitset as the set of
ids whose bits it sets, `Count[s]` as that set's size, and a scan over slot positions as a pass over the set.
It reads the order array as the whole DAG's drain, which is what `Reach.ofDag` builds. The word layout below
that reading, and `Reach.extend`'s splice of a new leaf into the order, stay on `dag-outside-the-model` and are
sampled by `Conformance.reachLaws` and the new `dag-boundaries-differential`. Modelling the words would prove
bit arithmetic that the reach laws already sample on every DAG they build, and modelling the splice would
re-prove the drain's step at an insertion point. Neither changes what a caller can rely on, so both are left
for a phase that needs them.

**D155.3 — `cut`'s band is kept, although `truncation_ok` does not need it.** The proof shows that the
checkpoint's node and everything after it already meet the contract the replay theorem stands on. A cut
without the band would therefore preserve every replay too. It would not preserve `firstBreakFrom`'s guarantee
that no node after the checkpoint names a parent the compacted DAG does not hold, and that guarantee is why the
band exists (Phase 288). The band stays, and the differential holds the extracted kept set equal to
production's, band included. Dropping it was considered and declined: it would trade a sampled integrity check
for a few nodes of storage, which is the wrong direction.

**D155.4 — `Dag.mergeBase`'s two implementations are one answer, proved.** Phase 388 made `deepest` size only
the maximal members of a common set that drains completely. Until now the proof was about Phase 158's version,
which sizes every member, and a differential held the two equal. `merge_base_now_is_merge_base` makes that a
theorem over any witnessed closure, and the proof does not depend on which branch the drain test takes. The
Phase 158 model stays the statement's subject, because `merge_base_maximal` and the divergence theorems are
phrased over it.

## 2026-10-14 — D154: `dirtyFromOp` closes over the diff's seeds, so the dirty set an op induces is complete; the composition with incremental evaluation is proved for the structural evaluator class in the one-map shape, and the cross-map prior stays the domain's

**Status:** Live

**Recorded by Phase 456. `src/Fuaran.Core.Propagation/Propagation.fs` (`seedsForOp`, `dirtyFromOp`,
`changedForOp`), `proofs/PropagationOps.fst` sections 5–6, `proofs/Propagation.fst` (`agree_on`,
`checks_on`, `evalfrom_agrees_on`), `proofs.json`, `proofs/coverage-exclusions.json`; rides the
